Fuel Price Hikes 2018

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
October has heralded a record breaking fuel price of over R17 per litre, for South Africans. Experts say it's going to hit just about every aspect of our economy.

Unique Selling Point:
The fuel levy is currently the fourth-biggest source of income for government after income tax, company tax and VAT.
It contributes 5% to national tax revenue.
It’s easy to collect and difficult to evade.
It is a large contributor to South Africa's high cost in fuel and looks like it is here to stay, generating over R 70 billion in government revenue per year.

Summary:
Since January this year South Africans have experienced 5 fuel hikes that have put our downward-spiraling economy into further perilous territory.
In September, it looked like there was going to be some relief as a 35 cents/l fuel increase was abated, and at the last minute we saw an increase of only 4,90 c/l.
But the Euphoria didn't last, October is seeing the fuel costs for ordinary consumers increase at around R1.00 /litre, pushing the cost of fuel to over R17,00 per litre.
What has driven South African fuel prices out of control, and are there more hikes to come? Who is responsible and can something be done to halt the drain on our pockets?
Is the fuel levy responsible for some of the high cost of our fuel?
Carte Blanche takes a journey with ordinary consumers who have been hard hit and it seems have no other choice, but to bite the bullet.

Further information:
Economist Mike Schussler unpacks the reasons for the high cost of fuel and why dipping into the Slate Levy Trust fund by the minister of energy, may not have been such a good idea, as consumers are now paying the price.

A global increase in the price of Brent Crude Oil and the looming sanctions by the US on Iran are impacting the global oil price, as well as a weakening rand which is what is increasing South Africa's fuel price so rapidly.

The average South African road user buys around 130 to 140 l of petrol a month, so at the new rate, they will be spending an additional R465 per month on fuel. Salaries aren't being increased to match these hikes, and so ordinary citizens are going to have to find other ways of making up the deficit on their budgets. Fuel Levies sit at around R5,30/l making up just under a third of our fuel price, but they are set annually and they collect around 6 Billion Rand a month or 72 Billion rand a year in taxes. This goes directly into the fiscus as a general tax, but SANRAL do see about 15 Billion rand of that from Treasury. Mike says, the fuel levy cannot be decreased at this stage, as this is a quick and efficient way for government to collect taxes. The fuel levy is currently the fourth biggest source of income for government after income tax and VAT. It contributes 5% to the national tax revenue.

More and more South Africans are compelled to use road transport which is dependent on fuel, as our railways have failed us, on a consumer level, as well as an industry level. About 75% of all produce is transported by road, which means that this fuel increase will have a direct result on our pockets in the end. It will also affect food production and food costs. Transportation makes up 11% of food costs, retailers will have to decide how much of this extra cost they can absorb and when they will ultimately pass it on to the consumer. Currently these kinds of increases could hurt retailers very badly, as there is underspending and the economy isn't growing. The overall impact is that we may be facing interest rate hikes by the end of the year, and we are waiting for our assessment from ratings agencies in October.

Leighton Beard from the AA, expands on how the cost of fuel impacts consumers, and with the holiday season coming up, there may be a lot fewer road trips for our citizens, what with tolls and an increase in fuel prices, long distance holidays may be a thing of the past. He looks at how South Africans can bring down their fuel spend. He emphasises that it's the poor South Africans that will suffer the most, especially if they are catching taxis, that are directly affected by the increase in fuel. Now many taxis might start overloading their taxis, so they can keep the cost of travel low, but at the same time they might be endangering more lives. He explains the impact of a possible other increase coming up in November.

Agricultural Economist, Wandile Sihlobo, gives us an insight into the impact on food production. This hike comes at a very bad time for the agricultural sector as it is now planting season, which means that fuel is a key driver, and even fertilisers contain oil and the cost of fertilisers has increased as well.

Mr Robert Maake, is the Director for Fuel Price Mechanisms, at the Department of Energy, and is responsible for setting the fuel price. He will explain how government sets the fuel price and what are the aspects that affect it's increase or decrease, He will speak to what makes up the cost of fuel and how the fuel levy price is set. Most people say the price may come down when the rand strengthens, but we put to him, will the consumers see the benefits of a decrease, as the decreases never really match the increases, rand for rand, that have occurred.

The story will be treated, as though it is a day in the life of Derek Watts on a Carte Blanche shoot, and the various transport, and food costs that are necessary for the shoot to take place, we will use this as beat points for story telling. We speak to general consumers and go out in the streets to where this is affecting the narrative of everyman. Dynamic interviews in cars while Derek is driving, as well as gopro footage from the interior and exterior of the car of cars and road users. Some dynamic links on various transport elements, as well as graphics.

Press Release:


The record breaking fuel prices of over R 17 a litre are hitting South Africans hard. The knock on effects are potentially devastating for our economy. Carte Blanche goes on the road to find out what’s behind the escalating cost of fuel.

Script:


VOX POPS: At petrol station the night before the fuel price went up.

Derek: it may seem like a quiet tuesday night but with the biggest fuel hike of the year looming the anger and frustration of the motorists here is palpable. They are fed up with filling up and their pockets are running dry.

Vox Pop:

VO: South Africans have experienced 5 fuel hikes since January this year with a record breaking increase, for the first time motorists will be paying over R17 a litre for unleaded petrol, inland.

Mike: If you look at the difference between the average motorists between march and october their monthly fuel spend is up with R465.

(Montage cars traffic lights …. night streaky traffic shots etc.. time lapses)

VO: Economist Mike Schussler has done some calculations and says in general South Africans are much poorer this year.

Mike: We spend about 60 billion a month as SA consumers. The petrol price as increased with 6 billion it’s a big chunk of people's disposable salary, it is a huge problem

VO: So our crew decided to do a little experiment and track the costs of our fuel on an average shoot around Gauteng:

Derek: Today we're going to see average consumption and what the bill is. I’m surprised we’re not all riding bicycles today.

Some Vox: Pops through the car window…. Lady who talks about the weakening rand and international fuel prices???

Derek: If you compare the consumption of this bakkie up front with a modern vehicle that’s more fuel efficient, the running costs are huge

VO: Someone who knows all about fuel economy is Layton Beard of the Automobile Association of South Africa.

Derek: Layton please don’t forget your seatbelt i know you don’t always think of these things.

VO: Our basic fuel price is R8,50, so what exactly makes up the rest of the cost?
(Show graphic)

Layton: You've got your basic fuel price and that’s what is affected mostly by international product prices and the increase in international oil prices and the rand us dollar exchange rate

Derek: Which is around the world

Layton: and then you have storage and transport costs and wholesale margins but then added on top of the fuel price
so about a 3rd of every liter of petrol you buy are these 2 levies, you've got the general fuel levy with is R3.37 at the moment and you’ve got the RAF levy which is R1.93 the general fuel money goes directly to the fiscus. They use it for social grants, to build schools, to buy school books] together they combine to make R5.30 exactly.

(Car transition wipe type effect - timelapse short)

Derek: I’ve been doing some research and the fuel levy is currently the 4th biggest source of income for government after income tax, company tax and VAT.

Mike: When you put petrol in tax is in it, it’s easy for government to collect, its over R6 billion a month that we collect from the taxes. We collect 4 billion from the road accident fund.

Derek: This is one of the busiest roadways linking Johannesburg to Gauteng and thousands of commuters are travelling a minimum of 100 kilometers a day on this road.. and now it will cost them R120,00 a day…. IT WAS SOMETHING LIKE THIS..…..It’s a lot of money

Derek: So, We’re going to meet up with Robert Maake who’s the director of fuel pricing for the Department of Energy

Derek: Exactly what factors affected the latest increase

Robert: There are 2 main factors namely the weakening of the rand against the dollar which contributed around 50 cents on both petrol and diesel and also the higher crude oil prices which had an impact on the petroleum prices, it contributed around 50 cents on petrol and around 72 cents on diesel

Layton: We saw in september when there was a lot of problems with emerging market currencies, SA rand was amongst it, the value of the rand against the us dollar slipped significantly in that month.

VO: We also know the impending sanctions by the US on Iran will lessen oil supplies and the Brent Crude Oil price is predicted to rise above $80 dollars per barrel, by year end. The general trend when it comes to fuel pricing at the pumps per country is, the wealthier a country the higher the price of fuel, the poorer, the cheaper the fuel

Derek: All our neighbors paying less than we do and they import the fuel from us.

TRANSITION

Robert: In our neighboring countries like Botswana and so on they don't have the fuel levy and the road accident fund which amount to more than R5 in our price. If you compare ourselves with countries like Botswana the economy is very small the population is very small, their demand is not the same as the demand we have here.

Derek: But Mr Maake the fuel levy and the road accident fund which are the problems in this country

Robert: We now have free tertiary education we have social grants and other things that government is funding and that money has to come from somewhere.

Layton: Let’s say we scrap the levies and together we're looking at R120 billion a year that these contribute to the general fiscus. If we take the 120 billion out of the fiskis where is government going to get that money because it still needs that revenue.

PEOPLE STREET TRANSITION

VO: The higher price of South African fuel has hit Sifiso’s printing business hard, he puts the blame squarely on governments shoulders.

VOX POP: Sfiso: I think they're trying to fix all the money they've eaten up and the taxpayers have to pay again for their mistakes

Mike: Government spending has been running uncontrollably forward in public servants. wages, corruption and overspending on many other aspects. if we never had to bail out SAA that’s 4 months of fuel taxes we didn’t have to pay.

Derek: Because of the fuel price increase our producer has limited us to a budget lunch at the Sylverspoon.

Hi, how you're doing? You're Sylvester from the Silver spoon. Great place you've got here. Could i have the chicken shwarma with salad

VO: Sylvester Kanono, owns this kiosk that is serving these excellent meals at a much lower cost, but can he keep this up?

Sylvester: When the fuel increases it affects us a lot, small businesses because it will mean our suppliers will up their pricing and it puts us in a difficult position.

Derek: This is the big test. The budget lunch isn’t bad for R30. The pita and the chips are good, and Sylvester said probably go up R5 in the next week or two.

Layton: When you look at a stimulus package as the president announced to revive the economy its going to be difficult in this environment where petrol is so expensive. People are really struggling,they are using illuminating paraffin for cooking, heating, lighting they're having to pay R1.24 more for their fuel than they did at the beginning of October.

VO: The agricultural sector will be even more hard hit, especially now during the planting season

Mike: In some goods we find the price knock on effect is twice, once from transport and once from the stuff its made from. When inflation comes, the reserve bank is going to increase interest rates.

Derek: Oil is in everything from toothpaste to fertilisers.

Frans: How much do you think it can be?

Derek: 50 cents

Frans: No this is R2 each

Derek: You serious?

Frans: I’m telling you. if you sell 50 cent you don’t buy nothing, just give people mahala, just take it, no commission for you and you've spent the petrol from here to town to come back to here


Derek: We might complain about filling our tanks and our cars but this is how most of the country travels, by taxi.

VO: Trains could be an alternative to the high cost of road transport.

Mike: We've seen a decline of more than 60% in the number of passengers on trains from 55 million a month to 20 million in a period of 8 years if you look at the cheap train ticket its 280 rand for a 50km monthly ticket, the same price on a taxi cost R1680.

VO: Even so, with another predicted fuel increase in November, South Africans have got the road mapped out for them, but government is looking at some interventions.

Robert: Some countries have what is known as the stabilization fund so they collect money from the motorists when the fuel price goes down they collect a percentage of that money put in that fund.

Derek: We pay in the end don’t we?

Robert: Of course, motorists will have to pay for it.

Derek: Have you started to monitor your own fuel consumption

Robert: I must share i tried to fill up my car on Tuesday before the deadline but i could only R1,000 which was for 63 liters and my car takes 85.

Derek: Are you thinking of downsizing?

Robert: I’m thinking of buying a bicycle.

VO: Well we’re back on our bicycle and it seems there’s no getting away from the increases that we’re experiencing so we have to bite the bullet and cut back on basically everything. Let’s see how much fuel we guzzled over our shoot?

Derek: Only did 222 Ks at 8,1 litres a 100 Ks at the present fuel price it comes to, well less than 310 rand, well that's just basic fuel price.

Derek: Layton please don’t forget your seatbelt i know you don’t always think of these things. VO: Our basic fuel price is R8,50, so what exactly makes up the rest of the cost? (Show graphic) Layton: You've got your basic fuel price and that’s what is affected mostly by international product prices and the increase in international oil prices and the rand us dollar exchange rate Derek: Which is around the world Layton: and then you have storage and transport costs and wholesale margins but then added on top of the fuel price so about a 3rd of every liter of petrol you buy are these 2 levies, you've got the general fuel levy with is R3.37 at the moment and you’ve got the RAF levy which is R1.93 the general fuel money goes directly to the fiscus. They use it for social grants, to build schools, to buy school books] together they combine to make R5.30 exactly. (Car transition wipe type effect - timelapse short) Derek: I’ve been doing some research and the fuel levy is currently the 4th biggest source of income for government after income tax, company tax and VAT. Mike: When you put petrol in tax is in it, it’s easy for government to collect, its over R6 billion a month that we collect from the taxes. We collect 4 billion from the road accident fund. Derek: This is one of the busiest roadways linking Johannesburg to Gauteng and thousands of commuters are travelling a minimum of 100 kilometers a day on this road.. and now it will cost them R120,00 a day…. IT WAS SOMETHING LIKE THIS..…..It’s a lot of money Derek: So, We’re going to meet up with Robert Maake who’s the director of fuel pricing for the Department of Energy Derek: Exactly what factors affected the latest increase Robert: There are 2 main factors namely the weakening of the rand against the dollar which contributed around 50 cents on both petrol and diesel and also the higher crude oil prices which had an impact on the petroleum prices, it contributed around 50 cents on petrol and around 72 cents on diesel Layton: We saw in september when there was a lot of problems with emerging market currencies, SA rand was amongst it, the value of the rand against the us dollar slipped significantly in that month. VO: We also know the impending sanctions by the US on Iran will lessen oil supplies and the Brent Crude Oil price is predicted to rise above $80 dollars per barrel, by year end. The general trend when it comes to fuel pricing at the pumps per country is, the wealthier a country the higher the price of fuel, the poorer, the cheaper the fuel Derek: All our neighbors paying less than we do and they import the fuel from us. TRANSITION Robert: In our neighboring countries like Botswana and so on they don't have the fuel levy and the road accident fund which amount to more than R5 in our price. If you compare ourselves with countries like Botswana the economy is very small the population is very small, their demand is not the same as the demand we have here. Derek: But Mr Maake the fuel levy and the road accident fund which are the problems in this country Robert: We now have free tertiary education we have social grants and other things that government is funding and that money has to come from somewhere. Layton: Let’s say we scrap the levies and together we're looking at R120 billion a year that these contribute to the general fiscus. If we take the 120 billion out of the fiskis where is government going to get that money because it still needs that revenue. PEOPLE STREET TRANSITION VO: The higher price of South African fuel has hit Sifiso’s printing business hard, he puts the blame squarely on governments shoulders. VOX POP: Sfiso: I think they're trying to fix all the money they've eaten up and the taxpayers have to pay again for their mistakes Mike: Government spending has been running uncontrollably forward in public servants. wages, corruption and overspending on many other aspects. if we never had to bail out SAA that’s 4 months of fuel taxes we didn’t have to pay. Derek: Because of the fuel price increase our producer has limited us to a budget lunch at the Sylverspoon. Hi, how you're doing? You're Sylvester from the Silver spoon. Great place you've got here. Could i have the chicken shwarma with salad VO: Sylvester Kanono, owns this kiosk that is serving these excellent meals at a much lower cost, but can he keep this up? Sylvester: When the fuel increases it affects us a lot, small businesses because it will mean our suppliers will up their pricing and it puts us in a difficult position. Derek: This is the big test. The budget lunch isn’t bad for R30. The pita and the chips are good, and Sylvester said probably go up R5 in the next week or two. Layton: When you look at a stimulus package as the president announced to revive the economy its going to be difficult in this environment where petrol is so expensive. People are really struggling,they are using illuminating paraffin for cooking, heating, lighting they're having to pay R1.24 more for their fuel than they did at the beginning of October. VO: The agricultural sector will be even more hard hit, especially now during the planting season Mike: In some goods we find the price knock on effect is twice, once from transport and once from the stuff its made from. When inflation comes, the reserve bank is going to increase interest rates. Derek: Oil is in everything from toothpaste to fertilisers. Frans: How much do you think it can be? Derek: 50 cents Frans: No this is R2 each Derek: You serious? Frans: I’m telling you. if you sell 50 cent you don’t buy nothing, just give people mahala, just take it, no commission for you and you've spent the petrol from here to town to come back to here Derek: We might complain about filling our tanks and our cars but this is how most of the country travels, by taxi. VO: Trains could be an alternative to the high cost of road transport. Mike: We've seen a decline of more than 60% in the number of passengers on trains from 55 million a month to 20 million in a period of 8 years if you look at the cheap train ticket its 280 rand for a 50km monthly ticket, the same price on a taxi cost R1680. VO: Even so, with another predicted fuel increase in November, South Africans have got the road mapped out for them, but government is looking at some interventions. Robert: Some countries have what is known as the stabilization fund so they collect money from the motorists when the fuel price goes down they collect a percentage of that money put in that fund. Derek: We pay in the end don’t we? Robert: Of course, motorists will have to pay for it. Derek: Have you started to monitor your own fuel consumption Robert: I must share i tried to fill up my car on Tuesday before the deadline but i could only R1,000 which was for 63 liters and my car takes 85. Derek: Are you thinking of downsizing? Robert: I’m thinking of buying a bicycle. VO: Well we’re back on our bicycle and it seems there’s no getting away from the increases that we’re experiencing so we have to bite the bullet and cut back on basically everything. Let’s see how much fuel we guzzled over our shoot? Derek: Only did 222 Ks at 8,1 litres a 100 Ks at the present fuel price it comes to, well less than 310 rand, well that's just basic fuel price.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): October has heralded a record breaking fuel price of over R17 per litre, for South Africans. Experts say it's going to hit just about every aspect of our economy.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The fuel levy is currently the fourth-biggest source of income for government after income tax, company tax and VAT. It contributes 5% to national tax revenue. It’s easy to collect and difficult to evade. It is a large contributor to South Africa's high cost in fuel and looks like it is here to stay, generating over R 70 billion in government revenue per year.
metadata.Summary: Since January this year South Africans have experienced 5 fuel hikes that have put our downward-spiraling economy into further perilous territory. In September, it looked like there was going to be some relief as a 35 cents/l fuel increase was abated, and at the last minute we saw an increase of only 4,90 c/l. But the Euphoria didn't last, October is seeing the fuel costs for ordinary consumers increase at around R1.00 /litre, pushing the cost of fuel to over R17,00 per litre. What has driven South African fuel prices out of control, and are there more hikes to come? Who is responsible and can something be done to halt the drain on our pockets? Is the fuel levy responsible for some of the high cost of our fuel? Carte Blanche takes a journey with ordinary consumers who have been hard hit and it seems have no other choice, but to bite the bullet.
metadata.Further information: Economist Mike Schussler unpacks the reasons for the high cost of fuel and why dipping into the Slate Levy Trust fund by the minister of energy, may not have been such a good idea, as consumers are now paying the price. A global increase in the price of Brent Crude Oil and the looming sanctions by the US on Iran are impacting the global oil price, as well as a weakening rand which is what is increasing South Africa's fuel price so rapidly. The average South African road user buys around 130 to 140 l of petrol a month, so at the new rate, they will be spending an additional R465 per month on fuel. Salaries aren't being increased to match these hikes, and so ordinary citizens are going to have to find other ways of making up the deficit on their budgets. Fuel Levies sit at around R5,30/l making up just under a third of our fuel price, but they are set annually and they collect around 6 Billion Rand a month or 72 Billion rand a year in taxes. This goes directly into the fiscus as a general tax, but SANRAL do see about 15 Billion rand of that from Treasury. Mike says, the fuel levy cannot be decreased at this stage, as this is a quick and efficient way for government to collect taxes. The fuel levy is currently the fourth biggest source of income for government after income tax and VAT. It contributes 5% to the national tax revenue. More and more South Africans are compelled to use road transport which is dependent on fuel, as our railways have failed us, on a consumer level, as well as an industry level. About 75% of all produce is transported by road, which means that this fuel increase will have a direct result on our pockets in the end. It will also affect food production and food costs. Transportation makes up 11% of food costs, retailers will have to decide how much of this extra cost they can absorb and when they will ultimately pass it on to the consumer. Currently these kinds of increases could hurt retailers very badly, as there is underspending and the economy isn't growing. The overall impact is that we may be facing interest rate hikes by the end of the year, and we are waiting for our assessment from ratings agencies in October. Leighton Beard from the AA, expands on how the cost of fuel impacts consumers, and with the holiday season coming up, there may be a lot fewer road trips for our citizens, what with tolls and an increase in fuel prices, long distance holidays may be a thing of the past. He looks at how South Africans can bring down their fuel spend. He emphasises that it's the poor South Africans that will suffer the most, especially if they are catching taxis, that are directly affected by the increase in fuel. Now many taxis might start overloading their taxis, so they can keep the cost of travel low, but at the same time they might be endangering more lives. He explains the impact of a possible other increase coming up in November. Agricultural Economist, Wandile Sihlobo, gives us an insight into the impact on food production. This hike comes at a very bad time for the agricultural sector as it is now planting season, which means that fuel is a key driver, and even fertilisers contain oil and the cost of fertilisers has increased as well. Mr Robert Maake, is the Director for Fuel Price Mechanisms, at the Department of Energy, and is responsible for setting the fuel price. He will explain how government sets the fuel price and what are the aspects that affect it's increase or decrease, He will speak to what makes up the cost of fuel and how the fuel levy price is set. Most people say the price may come down when the rand strengthens, but we put to him, will the consumers see the benefits of a decrease, as the decreases never really match the increases, rand for rand, that have occurred. The story will be treated, as though it is a day in the life of Derek Watts on a Carte Blanche shoot, and the various transport, and food costs that are necessary for the shoot to take place, we will use this as beat points for story telling. We speak to general consumers and go out in the streets to where this is affecting the narrative of everyman. Dynamic interviews in cars while Derek is driving, as well as gopro footage from the interior and exterior of the car of cars and road users. Some dynamic links on various transport elements, as well as graphics.
